title: The Colors of Venice
tagline: The last great master sets his canvas ablaze with color and light.

scenes.text: Venice, 1510. The city floats on the lagoon, and its school of painting is about to float above all others. A young student of the aged Bellini is developing a technique so revolutionary it will change painting forever — not what he paints, but how.

scenes.speaker: Titian
scenes.text: Bellini teaches us to build up the painting layer by layer: first the drawing, then the underpainting, then the color. I say: think in color from the first stroke. Let color carry the emotion, not the line.

challenge.fact: Titian (c. 1488–1576) worked for nearly 70 years, painting for Holy Roman Emperor Charles V, Philip II of Spain, and Pope Paul III. His late style — loose, almost abstract brushwork — was centuries ahead of its time.

scenes.text: Titian lived nearly a century and painted kings, popes, and emperors. Holy Roman Emperor Charles V reportedly stooped to pick up Titian's fallen brush — an honor no monarch had ever paid an artist.

scenes.speaker: Titian
scenes.text: I do not paint men. I paint the light that falls on them. And the light that falls on a cardinal's robe is not the same light that falls on a farmer's face — because the light remembers what kind of life it has touched.

challenge.instruction: Master Titian's famous Venetian palette — deep indigo backgrounds, crimson robes, and golden skin tones.
challenge.fact: Venetian painting was distinguished by its rich colour, applied in multiple glazed layers over days or weeks. Titian's reds — sometimes called 'Titian red' — were achieved with expensive vermilion and glazes of lake pigment.

challenge.instruction: Titian's Venice was famous for its madrigals. Arrange notes of a Renaissance vocal phrase — the music Titian heard daily.
challenge.fact: Venice's Basilica di San Marco had two organ lofts facing each other, inspiring the 'cori spezzati' style — antiphonal music where choirs answer each other across space. Giovanni Gabrieli developed this into orchestral writing.

scenes.text: Titian's final works — loose brushstrokes, patches of pure color — were centuries ahead of their time. He kept painting until his death at approximately 99, still pushing the boundaries of what paint could do.

challenge.instruction: Murano glassmakers arranged geometric forms to hide their secrets — matches can run in any direction, even diagonally. Clear 40 shapes.
challenge.fact: Venice ordered all glassmakers to the island of Murano in 1291 — ostensibly to prevent fires, really to contain the secrets of cristallo glass. Murano craftsmen held rare freedom: they could marry nobility and carry swords, but leaving the island was punishable by death.

challenge.instruction: Paint each section of the bowl with the right metal oxide glaze before firing.
challenge.fact: Venetian glassmakers on Murano pioneered cobalt blue glass using smalt — cobalt oxide imported from Saxony — becoming the dominant blue pigment in Renaissance Europe.

challenge.instruction: Bid on rare Renaissance goods at the Rialto Auction House. Win the starred items before your budget runs out.
challenge.fact: Venice's Rialto market was one of Europe's first commodity exchanges, trading silk, spices, and art from across the known world.

challenge.instruction: Titian painted at breakneck speed. Reassemble the fragments of his Assumption of the Virgin — swap tiles until the composition is whole.
challenge.fact: Titian's Assumption of the Virgin (1518) shattered every convention of Renaissance altarpiece painting. The Cardinal of Venice initially refused to accept it — then stood speechless before it.

challenge.instruction: You are the new curator of the Uffizi. Assign each Renaissance masterpiece to the room where it earns the greatest bonus and hit the target score.
challenge.fact: The Uffizi Gallery in Florence holds the finest concentration of Renaissance masterpieces in the world — Botticelli's Venus, da Vinci's Annunciation, and Titian's Venus of Urbino under one roof.

challenge.instruction: Recreate Titian's legendary crimson — a layered blend of vermilion and kermes lake that defined Venetian painting for a century.
challenge.fact: Titian's reds were so celebrated that 'rosso Tizianesco' became a byword for luminous crimson. He applied multiple thin glazes of kermes lake over a vermilion ground — a method only perfected over decades.
